name: CP2000
title: Proposed changes to your tax return
what: The income or payments reported to the IRS by employers, banks, brokers and others don't match what's on your return. The IRS is proposing changes, which usually means more tax, interest and possibly a penalty. It is not a bill and not a formal audit yet.
common: A missed 1099 (interest, dividends, freelance, stock sales)
Stock sales reported without cost basis
Retirement distributions or unemployment left off the return
todo: Compare every item on the notice to your records and your return
If you agree, sign the response form and pay or set up a payment plan
If you disagree in whole or part, send the response form with a signed explanation and documents
Don't file an amended return for these changes; respond to the notice instead
deadline: Respond by the date on the notice, usually 30 days. If you don't, the IRS sends a Statutory Notice of Deficiency, and the tax is assessed if you don't petition Tax Court in time.

name: CP2501
title: Income on your return doesn't match IRS records
what: An earlier, informal version of the CP2000. The IRS found a difference between your return and information it received, and is asking you to explain before it proposes changes.
common: Unreported 1099 or W-2 income
Income reported on a different line or form than the IRS expected
todo: Check whether the income is already included somewhere on your return
Reply with an explanation and supporting documents, or agree that it was missed
Respond even if you think it's already correct, so it doesn't move to a CP2000
deadline: Respond by the date on the notice to avoid a CP2000.

name: CP14
title: You have a balance due
what: The first bill for unpaid tax. It shows the tax, penalties and interest owed as of the notice date. Interest and late-payment penalties keep growing until it's paid.
common: Return filed without full payment
Estimated payments missed or applied to the wrong year
A change the IRS made after processing your return
todo: Check that the balance is right, including any payments you made
Pay in full by the due date, or apply for a payment plan
If you disagree, contact the IRS at the number on the notice
deadline: Pay by the date on the notice (usually 21 days) to limit extra interest and penalties.

name: CP501
title: Reminder: you still have a balance due
what: A follow-up reminder that a balance is still unpaid after an earlier notice. Interest and penalties are still being added.
common: A CP14 that wasn't paid or answered
todo: Pay the balance or set up a payment plan
Contact the IRS if you've already paid or disagree
deadline: Act by the date on the notice. Next comes a CP503.

name: CP503
title: Second reminder: balance due
what: An urgent second reminder that a balance is unpaid. Ignoring it moves you closer to a notice of intent to levy.
common: Earlier balance-due notices not paid or answered
todo: Pay now or set up a payment plan
Call the number on the notice if you can't pay in full
Get help if you're facing several years of balances
deadline: Act by the date on the notice. Next comes a CP504.

name: CP504
title: Notice of intent to levy
what: The IRS intends to seize (levy) your state tax refund to pay the balance, and warns it may levy other property or rights. It can also lead to a federal tax lien.
common: Balance unpaid after CP14, CP501 and CP503
todo: Pay in full, or set up a payment plan right away
If you can't pay, ask about hardship status or other options
Get professional help before a final levy notice arrives
deadline: Act by the date on the notice. The next step is usually a final notice with appeal rights (LT11 or Letter 1058).

name: LT11 / Letter 1058
title: Final notice of intent to levy and your right to a hearing
what: The IRS's final notice before it can levy wages, bank accounts and other assets. It also gives you the right to a Collection Due Process (CDP) hearing with the IRS Independent Office of Appeals.
common: Unpaid balances after earlier notices
todo: Pay in full or arrange a payment plan
To protect your appeal rights, file Form 12153 (Request for a Collection Due Process hearing) on time
Talk to an Enrolled Agent or other tax professional now
deadline: You have 30 days from the notice date to request a CDP hearing. Missing it limits your options.

name: CP90
title: Final notice of intent to levy
what: A final notice that the IRS intends to levy your assets, such as wages, bank accounts, Social Security or other income, and your right to a Collection Due Process hearing.
common: Unpaid balances after earlier notices
todo: Pay or arrange a payment plan
File Form 12153 to request a hearing if you disagree or need time
Get professional help right away
deadline: 30 days from the notice date to request a Collection Due Process hearing.

name: CP3219A / Letter 3219
title: Statutory Notice of Deficiency
what: The IRS has determined you owe additional tax and is formally telling you of your right to challenge it in U.S. Tax Court. It often follows an unanswered CP2000 or an audit you didn't agree with.
common: No response to a CP2000
Audit changes you didn't agree to
todo: Decide whether you agree with the changes
If you disagree, file a petition with the U.S. Tax Court before the deadline
Don't ignore it: once the deadline passes the tax is assessed
deadline: 90 days from the notice date to petition Tax Court (150 days if addressed to you outside the U.S.). The deadline cannot be extended.

name: CP11
title: We changed your return: you owe money
what: The IRS found a math or calculation error on your return, corrected it, and you now owe tax.
common: Miscalculated credits (child tax credit, earned income credit)
Recovery or stimulus credit errors
Arithmetic errors
todo: Compare the IRS's changes to your return
If you agree, pay or set up a payment plan
If you disagree, contact the IRS within 60 days and they'll reverse the change, though they may then examine it further
deadline: 60 days from the notice date to dispute the change.

name: CP12
title: We changed your return: your refund changed
what: The IRS corrected one or more errors on your return. Your refund is now different, or you now get a refund instead of owing.
common: Miscalculated credits
Withholding or estimated payment amounts entered incorrectly
todo: Review the changes against your return
If you agree, you usually don't need to reply, but follow the instructions on your notice
If you disagree, contact the IRS within 60 days
deadline: 60 days from the notice date to dispute the change.

name: CP59
title: You didn't file a tax return
what: IRS records show you didn't file a return for the year shown, and you may need to. Not filing can lead to penalties and the IRS filing a substitute return for you.
common: A return was never filed
A return was filed under a different SSN or name
A return was sent but not processed
todo: File the missing return right away
If you already filed, send a copy and the date filed
If you weren't required to file, explain why using the response form
deadline: Respond by the date on the notice.

name: CP05
title: We're reviewing your return
what: The IRS is reviewing your return to verify income, withholding, credits or business income before issuing your refund. It does not mean you did something wrong.
common: Random or automated verification of withholding and credits
todo: You usually don't need to reply unless the IRS asks for more information
Keep your W-2s, 1099s and records handy
Wait for the follow-up notice
deadline: No response required. Review typically takes several weeks.

name: CP75
title: Audit: documents needed for credits
what: The IRS is auditing your return and holding part or all of your refund until you prove eligibility for credits such as the Earned Income Tax Credit, or certain deductions.
common: Earned Income Tax Credit
Child tax credit or dependent claims
Business income on Schedule C
todo: Gather the documents listed (school or medical records showing children lived with you, business records)
Send them by the deadline using the enclosed form
Get help if you're unsure what proves eligibility
deadline: Respond by the date on the notice, usually 30 days.

name: Letter 5071C
title: Verify your identity
what: The IRS received a return with your name and SSN and needs you to confirm it was you who filed it, to protect against identity theft. Your return and refund are on hold until you verify.
common: Possible identity theft
Changes in your filing pattern
todo: Verify online at the IRS identity verification site listed in the letter, or by phone
Have the letter, your prior-year and current-year returns and supporting documents ready
If you didn't file the return, say so: it may be identity theft
deadline: Verify as soon as possible. Your refund won't be released until you do.

name: Letter 4883C
title: Verify your identity by phone
what: As with Letter 5071C, the IRS needs to confirm your identity before processing a return filed under your name, but asks you to call.
common: Possible identity theft
todo: Call the number in the letter (only that number)
Have the letter, the return in question and your prior-year return ready
deadline: Call as soon as possible; processing stops until you do.

name: Letter 12C
title: We need more information to process your return
what: Your return is missing information or forms, so the IRS can't finish processing it.
common: Missing Form 8962 for Marketplace health insurance (Form 1095-A)
Missing W-2 or withholding information
Missing schedules
todo: Send the requested form or information
Include a copy of the letter with your response
deadline: Respond by the date in the letter, usually 20 days, or your refund may be reduced.

name: Letter 566
title: Correspondence audit: first contact
what: The IRS is examining (auditing) specific items on your return by mail and is asking you to send documents to support them.
common: Deductions or credits that need proof
Business expenses
todo: Read which items are being examined
Send organized copies of receipts and records, never originals
Consider having an Enrolled Agent represent you
deadline: Respond by the date in the letter.

name: Letter 525
title: Proposed audit changes
what: After examining your return, the IRS is proposing changes, usually additional tax. You can agree, or disagree and provide more information or request an appeal.
common: Documents sent during an audit weren't enough
No response to an earlier audit letter
todo: Review the examination report
Sign the agreement form if you agree
If you disagree, send more information or request an Appeals conference
deadline: Usually 30 days from the letter date. After that, a Statutory Notice of Deficiency may follow.

name: CP49
title: Your refund was applied to a tax debt
what: The IRS used all or part of your refund to pay a balance you owe for another tax year.
common: Prior-year balance due
todo: Check which year the refund was applied to
If any refund remains, it will be sent separately
Contact the IRS if you think the debt was already paid
deadline: No response required unless you disagree.

name: CP71C
title: Annual reminder of a balance due
what: A yearly reminder that you still have an unpaid balance, which continues to grow with interest and penalties.
common: An older balance that's been in collection or put on hold
todo: Pay what you can or set up a payment plan
Ask about options if you can't pay
deadline: Act as soon as possible to keep interest and penalties from growing.

name: CP521
title: Installment agreement payment reminder
what: A reminder of your monthly payment under an existing IRS payment plan, and your remaining balance.
common: Active installment agreement
todo: Make your payment by the due date
Consider setting up automatic payments
deadline: Pay by the due date shown.

name: CP523
title: Intent to end your payment plan and levy
what: The IRS intends to terminate your installment agreement, usually because payments were missed or new taxes went unpaid, and then levy your assets.
common: Missed monthly payments
A new balance due
Unfiled returns
todo: Bring payments current right away
File any missing returns
Call the IRS or get help to reinstate the agreement
deadline: Act by the date on the notice. You may have the right to appeal the termination.

name: CP161
title: Business balance due
what: Your business owes money for the tax period shown, often because a return was processed with an unpaid balance, penalties or a math error.
common: Late filing or late payment penalties
Payroll tax deposits short or late
Math errors on the business return
todo: Check the balance against your payment records
Pay or set up a business payment plan
Request penalty relief if you qualify (for example, first-time abatement)
deadline: Pay by the date on the notice to avoid more interest and penalties.

name: CP2100 / CP2100A
title: Backup withholding: incorrect payee TINs
what: Sent to businesses that file 1099s. Some of the names and taxpayer ID numbers you reported don't match IRS records, and you may need to start backup withholding on those payees.
common: Contractors who gave a wrong SSN/EIN
Name changes or typos on 1099s
todo: Compare the list to your records
Send a B-notice to each listed payee with a new W-9
Start backup withholding (24%) if a payee doesn't respond in time
deadline: Send B-notices within 15 business days of receiving the notice.

name: CP575
title: Your new EIN (Employer Identification Number)
what: Confirmation that the IRS assigned an EIN to your business. Banks and others often ask for this letter. It isn't a problem notice.
common: Applying for an EIN online, by fax or by mail
todo: Keep it with your permanent business records
If you lose it, ask the IRS for Letter 147C to confirm your EIN
deadline: No response required.

name: CP01
title: Your identity theft claim was confirmed
what: The IRS confirmed your identity theft report and placed a protective marker on your tax account. It's informational, not a bill, and no reply is needed.
common: You filed an identity theft affidavit (Form 14039)
Someone else filed a return using your Social Security number
todo: Keep the notice with your tax records
Keep filing your returns as usual
Watch for an Identity Protection PIN (IP PIN) in the mail each year and enter it on your return; returns filed without it will be rejected
deadline: No response required.

name: CP01H
title: Return not processed: SSN listed as belonging to someone who died
what: The IRS couldn't process your return because Social Security Administration records show that a Social Security number on it belongs to a person who died before the tax year. The account is locked until the records are fixed. It is not a bill.
common: An error in Social Security Administration death records
A typo in a Social Security number on the return
A return filed for someone who has died, using the wrong year or filing setup
todo: Check every Social Security number on the return against the cards
If SSA's records are wrong, contact the Social Security Administration to have them corrected
Once corrected, follow the notice instructions to file or refile the return
deadline: Act by the date on the notice. Your return and any refund stay on hold until the records are corrected.

name: CP04
title: You may qualify to defer tax because of military service
what: You served, or are serving, in a combat zone, contingency operation or hazardous duty area, and you may qualify to delay paying tax that is due. It is not a bill, and replying is optional.
common: Military service in a combat zone or qualified hazardous duty area
Support of a contingency operation
todo: Read the notice to see which tax period it covers
If you want the deferment, complete Form 15109 (Request for Tax Deferment)
Send it with proof of your service dates by the date on the notice
deadline: Optional, but send Form 15109 by the date on the notice if you want the deferment.

name: CP05B
title: Send documents before we release your refund
what: The IRS is holding your refund until you send documents that verify the income and withholding on your return. It is not a bill, but your refund won't be released until you respond.
common: Withholding on your return doesn't match what employers reported
Random or automated income verification
Missing W-2s or 1099s
todo: Gather copies of the documents listed in the notice, such as W-2s, 1099s and pay stubs
Send them with the voucher from the notice to the address shown
Keep copies and proof of mailing
deadline: Respond by the date on the notice. Your refund stays on hold until the IRS gets your documents.

name: CP07
title: Your refund is on hold for review
what: The IRS is holding your refund while it reviews treaty benefits or itemized deductions (Schedule A) on your return. It is not a bill and no reply is needed right now.
common: Itemized deductions on Schedule A
Tax treaty benefits claimed on the return
todo: You may not need to reply now, but read the notice carefully and keep it with your records
Don't file a second copy of your return; it slows the review
Gather receipts and records in case the IRS asks for them
deadline: No response required. Respond only if a follow-up letter asks for information.

name: CP08
title: You may qualify for the Additional Child Tax Credit
what: IRS records show you may be able to claim the Additional Child Tax Credit, the refundable part of the Child Tax Credit, but you didn't. It is not a bill; it's a chance at a larger refund.
common: You have a qualifying child but didn't claim the credit
The credit was left off when the return was prepared
todo: Complete the Form 15110 worksheet included with the notice
If you have at least one qualifying child, send Form 15110 and Schedule 8812
Send it through the IRS Document Upload Tool or by mail, as the notice explains
deadline: Optional. Respond by the date on the notice if you want the credit.

name: CP09
title: You may qualify for the Earned Income Credit
what: IRS records show you may be able to claim the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), a refundable credit for workers with low to moderate income and qualifying children, but you didn't. It is not a bill.
common: You have a qualifying child and earned income but didn't claim the credit
The credit was missed when the return was prepared
todo: Complete the EITC eligibility worksheet included with the notice
If you qualify, sign and send it through the IRS Document Upload Tool or by mail
If you don't qualify, no reply is needed
deadline: Optional. Respond by the date on the notice if you want the credit.

name: CP10
title: We changed the amount carried to next year's taxes
what: The IRS fixed a calculation error on your return, which changed the overpayment you asked to apply to next year's estimated tax. It is not a bill, but less money may be credited to next year.
common: A math or calculation error on the return
An error in the credits or payments claimed
todo: Read the explanation of the change
Increase next year's estimated payments if needed, so you don't get an underpayment penalty
Contact the IRS at the number on the notice if you disagree
deadline: Contact the IRS by the date on the notice if you disagree.

name: CP13
title: We changed your return: no balance due
what: The IRS corrected an error on your return. After the change you don't owe anything and you don't get a refund. It is not a bill.
common: A math or calculation error
An error in a credit or deduction amount
todo: Compare the change to your copy of the return
If you agree, no reply is needed
If you disagree, call the number on the notice by the date shown
deadline: No response required if you agree. If you disagree, contact the IRS by the date on the notice, usually within 60 days.

name: CP16
title: We changed your return and used your refund to pay other debts
what: The IRS corrected an error on your return, and some or all of your refund went to pay other tax you or your spouse owe. It is not a bill.
common: A math or calculation error on the return
An unpaid tax balance from another year
A balance owed by your spouse
todo: Review the change and how the refund was applied
Contact the IRS by the date on the notice if you disagree
If the refund went to your spouse's debt, ask whether Form 8379 (Injured Spouse Allocation) can get your share back
deadline: Contact the IRS by the date on the notice if you disagree.

name: CP21A
title: We made the change you asked for: you owe money
what: The IRS made the change you requested, usually from an amended return, and you now owe tax. This is a bill, and interest keeps growing until it's paid.
common: An amended return (Form 1040-X) that added income
A credit removed at your request
A correction you or your preparer requested
todo: Compare the change to the amended return you filed
Pay by the date on the payment coupon, or set up a payment plan
Ask about penalty relief (reasonable cause, or first-time abatement if it wasn't applied automatically)
Contact the IRS if you disagree with the change
deadline: Pay by the date on the notice to limit extra interest and penalties.

name: CP21B
title: We made the change you asked for: refund coming
what: The IRS made the change you requested and you are getting a refund, usually within 2 to 3 weeks. It is not a bill.
common: An amended return that lowered your tax
A credit or deduction added at your request
todo: Check that the refund amount matches what you expected
No reply is needed if you agree
Contact the IRS if you disagree or the refund doesn't arrive
deadline: No response required unless you disagree.

name: CP21C
title: We made the change you asked for: no balance due
what: The IRS made the change you requested. After the change you don't owe anything and you don't get a refund. It is not a bill.
common: An amended return or correction you requested
A credit or deduction change that offset an amount you owed
todo: Check that the change matches what you asked for
No reply is needed if you agree
Call the number on the notice if you disagree
deadline: No response required unless you disagree.

name: CP21E
title: Your audit changes were processed
what: The IRS made changes to your account after an audit. Depending on the result, you may owe money, get a refund, or have a zero balance. If the notice shows a balance due, it is a bill.
common: An audit that ended with changes to your return
Changes you agreed to during an audit
todo: Compare the notice to the audit report you received
Pay any balance by the date on the payment coupon, or set up a payment plan
Contact the IRS if you disagree
If you have new documents that weren't considered, ask about audit reconsideration (a request to reopen the audit)
deadline: If you owe, pay by the date on the notice to limit interest and penalties.

name: CP22A
title: We made the change you asked for: you owe money
what: The IRS changed your return as you requested, and you now owe tax. This is a bill, and interest keeps growing until it's paid.
common: An amended return or correction that increased your tax
A request to remove a credit or deduction
todo: Check that the change matches what you asked for
Pay by the date on the payment coupon, or set up a payment plan
Ask about penalty relief (reasonable cause, or first-time abatement if it wasn't applied automatically)
Contact the IRS if you disagree
deadline: Pay by the date on the notice to limit extra interest and penalties.

name: CP23
title: Your estimated payments don't match: you owe money
what: The estimated tax payments you claimed on your return don't match the payments the IRS has on record, so you owe money. This is a bill.
common: A payment applied to the wrong tax year
A payment made under your spouse's Social Security number
A missed or bounced payment
A typo in the amount claimed
todo: Compare your bank records with the payments listed on the notice (dates, amounts, year, Social Security number)
If the IRS is right, pay or set up a payment plan
If you have proof of a missing payment, contact the IRS by the date shown
Ask about penalty relief (reasonable cause, or first-time abatement if it wasn't applied automatically)
deadline: Pay or contact the IRS by the date on the notice to limit extra interest and penalties.

name: CP24
title: Your estimated payments don't match: refund coming
what: The estimated tax payments you claimed don't match the IRS records, but you still have an overpayment. The IRS changed your return, and any remaining refund usually arrives in 4 to 6 weeks if you owe no other debts. It is not a bill.
common: A payment applied to a different tax year
A payment missed or made under your spouse's number
A typo in the amount claimed
todo: Compare your payment records with the notice
If a payment is missing, contact the IRS with proof
If you agree, no reply is needed
deadline: No response required unless you disagree.

name: CP25
title: Your estimated payments don't match: no balance due
what: The estimated tax payments you claimed don't match the IRS records. After the correction you don't owe anything and you don't get a refund. It is not a bill.
common: A payment applied to a different tax year
A payment made under your spouse's number
A typo in the amount claimed
todo: Compare your payment records with the notice
No reply is needed if you agree
If you disagree, contact the IRS with proof of payment by the date shown
deadline: No response required if you agree. If you disagree, contact the IRS by the date on the notice.

name: CP27
title: You may qualify for the Earned Income Credit (no children)
what: IRS records show you may qualify for the Earned Income Tax Credit for workers without a qualifying child, but you didn't claim it. It is not a bill; it's a chance at a larger refund.
common: You had low to moderate earned income and no qualifying child
The credit was missed when the return was prepared
todo: Complete the eligibility worksheet included with the notice
If you qualify, sign and date it and mail it in the envelope provided
If you don't qualify, no reply is needed
deadline: Optional. Respond by the date on the notice if you want the credit.

name: CP30
title: Penalty for not paying enough tax during the year
what: The IRS charged a penalty because you didn't pay enough tax during the year through withholding or estimated payments. The penalty may reduce your refund or add to what you owe.
common: Not enough tax withheld from your pay
Estimated payments missed or too small
Income that came in unevenly during the year
todo: Check whether an exception on Form 2210, or calculating based on when income came in (the annualized method), lowers the penalty
Ask about penalty relief (reasonable cause, or first-time abatement if it wasn't applied automatically)
Adjust this year's withholding or estimated payments so it doesn't happen again
deadline: Pay any balance or contact the IRS by the date on the notice.

name: CP39
title: Your spouse's refund was used to pay your tax debt
what: The IRS used a refund belonging to your spouse or former spouse to pay your past-due tax. Some balance may still remain. It is informational, not a new bill.
common: You owed tax from an earlier year
A joint return produced a refund that was applied to your debt
todo: Review your account to see what balance, if any, is left
Call the IRS if you disagree
Keep bank records and any amended returns handy if you call
deadline: No response required unless you disagree. Any remaining balance still needs to be paid.

name: CP42
title: Your refund was used to pay your spouse's tax debt
what: The IRS used your refund to pay your spouse's past-due federal tax. It is not a bill.
common: Your spouse owed tax from another year
You filed a joint return with a spouse who has a tax debt
todo: Review the amount that was applied
If part of the refund was yours on a joint return, consider Form 8379 (Injured Spouse Allocation) to recover your share
Call the IRS if you disagree
deadline: No response required unless you disagree or want to file Form 8379.

name: CP45
title: We couldn't apply your overpayment to next year
what: You asked the IRS to apply part of your overpayment to next year's estimated tax, but it couldn't apply all of it. It is not a bill, but you may need to pay more estimated tax.
common: The overpayment was smaller than expected after IRS changes
Part of it went to another tax debt
todo: Review how much was actually carried forward
Increase this year's estimated payments to avoid an underpayment penalty
Contact the IRS if you think more of the overpayment should have carried forward
deadline: No response required, but adjust your estimated payments promptly.

name: CP51A
title: We figured your tax for you: you owe money
what: You asked the IRS to calculate your tax, and the result is that you owe money. This is a bill.
common: You filed a return and asked the IRS to compute the tax
Withholding didn't cover the tax
todo: Review the IRS calculation
Pay by the date shown, or set up a payment plan
Ask about penalty relief (reasonable cause, or first-time abatement if it wasn't applied automatically)
Contact the IRS if you disagree
deadline: Pay by the date on the notice to avoid more interest and penalties.

name: CP53
title: We can't direct deposit your refund
what: The IRS couldn't deposit your refund into the bank account on your return, so it is mailing a paper check. It is not a bill.
common: A closed or wrong bank account number
The account name doesn't match the name on the return
todo: You may not need to reply, but check the notice against your records and keep it on file
Make sure your mailing address is current
Call the IRS if the check hasn't arrived within 4 weeks
deadline: No response required.

name: CP60
title: We moved a payment off your account: you now owe
what: A payment was applied to your account by mistake, and the IRS moved it to where it belonged. This left a balance on your account, so this is a bill.
common: A payment entered under the wrong Social Security number or tax year
A payment that belonged to someone else
todo: Find out where the payment should have gone
If it really belongs on this account, contact the IRS with proof of payment
Otherwise pay by the date shown, or set up a payment plan
deadline: Pay or contact the IRS by the date on the notice to limit interest and penalties.

name: CP62
title: We applied your payment
what: The IRS confirms it applied a payment or credit to your account. It is a confirmation, not a new bill, but it may show a remaining balance.
common: A payment you made
A credit moved from another year
todo: Check that the payment was applied to the right year
If a balance remains, pay by the date shown or set up a payment plan
If a refund is shown, no reply is needed
deadline: No response required unless a balance remains; then pay by the date on the notice.

name: CP63
title: Your refund is on hold until you file missing returns
what: The IRS is holding your refund because one or more earlier returns haven't been filed and it believes you'll owe tax on them. It is not a bill.
common: A return from a prior year was never filed
A return was filed but not processed or was lost
todo: File the missing returns right away
If you already filed or didn't need to, explain that in your reply
Keep copies of everything you send
deadline: Respond by the date on the notice. If you don't, the IRS may prepare a return for you (CP2566), usually with a higher tax.

name: CP80
title: We have payments but no return
what: The IRS has payments or credits on your account for a tax year but hasn't received your return. It is not a bill.
common: The return was never filed
The return was lost in the mail or filed under a different number
todo: File the signed return to the address on the notice
If you already filed, send a signed copy
Keep proof of mailing
deadline: Respond by the date on the notice. If you don't, the IRS may prepare a return for you (CP2566).

name: CP81
title: You may lose a refund: we have payments but no return
what: The IRS has payments or credits on your account but no return, and time to claim a refund is almost up. It is not a bill, but if you don't file soon you lose the money.
common: The return was never filed
The return was lost or filed under the wrong number
todo: File the return immediately if you were required to file or want the refund
If you already filed, send a signed copy
Keep proof of mailing
deadline: File right away. Once the deadline passes, you lose the right to the refund.

name: CP88
title: Your refund is on hold until you file missing returns
what: The IRS is holding your refund because it has no record of one or more earlier returns and believes you'll owe tax on them. It is not a bill.
common: A prior-year return was never filed
A return was filed but not processed
todo: File the missing returns right away
If you already filed or didn't have to, explain that in your reply
Keep copies of what you send
deadline: Respond by the date on the notice. If you don't, the IRS may prepare a return for you (CP2566).

name: CP102
title: We changed your payroll tax return: you owe money
what: The IRS found a calculation error on your payroll tax return, such as Form 941 or 944, and you now owe money. This is a bill.
common: Math errors on the return
Wages, tax or deposits reported incorrectly
Deposits applied to the wrong quarter
todo: Compare the IRS figures to your return and payroll records
Pay by the date on the payment coupon, or set up a payment plan
If you disagree, contact the IRS within 10 days of the notice date
Ask about penalty relief (reasonable cause, or first-time abatement if it wasn't applied automatically)
deadline: Contact the IRS within 10 days if you disagree. Otherwise pay by the date on the notice, or more balance-due notices follow.

name: CP142
title: Your information returns were filed late
what: The IRS says your information returns, such as W-2s or 1099s, were filed late, which can lead to a penalty. It is not a bill yet; it asks for an explanation.
common: W-2s or 1099s filed after the deadline
An extension that wasn't on file
Returns filed under the wrong business name or EIN
todo: Gather proof of when you filed and any extension you had
Reply within 30 days with the requested information, a copy of the late return and the notice
Explain any reasonable cause for filing late, which can prevent the penalty
deadline: Respond within 30 days of the notice date, or a late-filing penalty may be charged.

name: CP143
title: We accepted your explanation for late information returns
what: The IRS accepted your explanation for filing information returns late and is not charging a penalty for it. It is not a bill.
common: You answered a CP142 with a good explanation
Proof that the returns were filed on time or under an extension
todo: You may not need to reply, but check the notice against your records and keep it on file
Keep the notice with your business records
Contact the IRS if a penalty for the same returns still shows on a later notice
deadline: No response required.

name: CP153
title: We can't direct deposit your refund
what: The IRS can't deposit your refund or credit into the bank account you gave, so it is mailing a paper check. It is not a bill.
common: A closed or wrong bank account
The name on the account doesn't match the return
todo: You may not need to reply, but check the notice against your records and keep it on file
Make sure your mailing address is current
Call the IRS if the check hasn't arrived within 4 weeks
deadline: No response required.

name: CP163
title: Reminder: you still owe tax
what: A reminder that you still owe tax, penalties and interest. This is a bill, and interest keeps growing until it's paid.
common: An earlier balance-due notice that wasn't paid
Penalties and interest added since the last notice
todo: Check that the balance is right, including any payments you made
Pay, or set up a payment plan
Ask about penalty relief (reasonable cause, or first-time abatement if it wasn't applied automatically)
deadline: Pay by the date on the notice to limit extra interest and penalties.

name: CP166
title: Your payment plan payment bounced
what: Your monthly payment plan payment couldn't be taken because there wasn't enough money in the bank account. It is not a new bill, but your payment plan is at risk.
common: Not enough money in the account on the withdrawal date
A closed or changed bank account
todo: Add enough money to the account to cover the payment and any fees
Contact the IRS to make the missed payment
Keep future payments on time so the payment plan isn't ended
deadline: Act right away to keep your payment plan from defaulting.

name: CP171
title: Reminder: you still owe tax
what: A reminder that you still owe tax, penalties and interest. This is a bill, and interest keeps growing until it's paid.
common: An earlier balance-due notice that wasn't paid
Penalties and interest added since the last notice
todo: Check that the balance is right
Pay, or set up a payment plan
Contact the IRS if you've already paid or disagree
deadline: Pay by the date on the notice to limit extra interest and penalties.

name: CP188
title: Your refund is on hold while we check for other debts
what: The IRS is holding your refund while it checks whether you owe other taxes. It is not a bill.
common: Possible unpaid tax from another year or another account
A balance on a joint or related account being checked
todo: You may not need to reply now, but read the notice carefully and keep it with your records
Read the notice for how long the review will take
Watch for a follow-up notice
deadline: No response required.

name: CP231
title: Your refund check was returned: update your address
what: Your refund or credit was returned to the IRS as undeliverable. It is not a bill, but you need to update your address to get the money.
common: You moved and didn't update your address
An error in the address on the return
todo: Call the IRS or return the contact section of the notice with your current address
Consider filing Form 8822 (Change of Address)
Watch for the reissued check
deadline: Respond as soon as possible so the refund can be reissued.

name: CP237
title: We issued a replacement refund check
what: The IRS issued a new refund check to replace an earlier one. It is not a bill.
common: The original check expired without being cashed
The original check was lost or returned
todo: Destroy any expired check you still have
Cash the new check when it arrives
Call the IRS if the new check doesn't arrive within a few weeks
deadline: No response required.

name: CP259
title: Your business didn't file a required return
what: The IRS has no record that your business filed a required tax return. It is not a bill, but you need to file or explain.
common: A return was never filed
A return filed under a different business name or EIN
The business closed without telling the IRS
todo: File the return right away, electronically if you can
Send back the response form explaining why it was late or isn't required
If you filed in the last 4 weeks under the same name and EIN, you can disregard the notice
deadline: Respond by the date on the notice. If you don't, the IRS may prepare the return for you and assess tax and penalties.

name: CP261
title: Your S corporation election was approved
what: The IRS accepted your Form 2553, so your business is taxed as an S corporation. It is not a bill.
common: You filed Form 2553 to elect S corporation status
An election filed late that the IRS accepted
todo: Keep the notice permanently with your corporate records as proof of the election
Check that the effective date is the one you wanted
Contact the IRS if the effective date or tax year shown is wrong
deadline: No response required.

name: CP504B
title: Notice of intent to levy: business
what: Your business has an unpaid balance and the IRS intends to take (levy) its property or rights to property, and may file a federal tax lien. This is a bill.
common: Business balance unpaid after earlier notices
Payroll or other business taxes not paid
todo: Pay right away, or arrange a payment plan, an offer in compromise (a settlement for less) or hardship status
Call the IRS if you disagree; you can also request a Collection Appeals Program review
Check whether you've already received a final notice with hearing rights (LT11 or Letter 1058)
Ask about penalty relief (reasonable cause, or first-time abatement if it wasn't applied automatically)
deadline: Act immediately. The next step is a final notice with hearing rights (LT11 or Letter 1058), then levy.

name: CP268
title: We changed your business return: you have a credit
what: The IRS corrected an error on your business return, and the change gives you an overpayment. It is not a bill.
common: A math or calculation error on the return
Payments or credits not counted correctly
todo: Compare the change to your return
Within 30 days, call to ask for a refund check or to apply the credit to other taxes
Contact the IRS if you disagree
deadline: Call within 30 days if you want to direct how the credit is used.

name: CP276A
title: Your payroll deposit schedule had errors: penalty waived
what: The tax liability schedule you filed with your payroll return (Schedule B or Form 945-A) was wrong. The IRS waived the deposit penalty this time. It is not a bill.
common: Liabilities listed by the wrong payroll date
Schedule totals that don't match the return
todo: Review how tax was listed by payroll date
Fix your deposit tracking so future schedules are accurate
Make sure future Schedule B or Form 945-A totals match the return; the penalty may not be waived next time
deadline: No response required.

name: CP276B
title: Your payroll deposits were made incorrectly: penalty waived
what: Your payroll tax deposits weren't made the right way or on time, but the IRS waived the penalty this time. It is not a bill.
common: Deposits made late or on the wrong schedule
Deposits made by the wrong method
todo: Review your deposit timing and schedule
Make sure current deposits are on time
Learn whether you are a monthly or semiweekly depositor; the penalty may not be waived next time
deadline: No response required.

name: CP282
title: Your partnership may need foreign partner withholding forms
what: Your partnership return (Form 1065) shows foreign partners, so the partnership may need to file withholding forms for them. It is not a bill.
common: Foreign partners listed on the partnership return
Partner addresses or tax ID details that suggest a foreign partner
todo: If the partnership owes withholding, file the required forms, such as Forms 8804, 8805 and 8813
If not, write "not liable" on the notice and mail it back
If you already filed them, list the forms filed and mail the notice back
deadline: Respond by the date on the notice.

name: CP297
title: Final notice of intent to levy federal payments
what: The IRS intends to take (levy) federal payments owed to your business, such as government contract payments, to pay your tax debt. It is your last notice before the levy and gives you the right to a hearing. This is a bill.
common: Unpaid business taxes after earlier notices
No payment plan in place
todo: Request a Collection Due Process hearing with Form 12153 within 30 days
Pay in full, or set up a payment plan or another option
Ask about penalty relief (reasonable cause, or first-time abatement if it wasn't applied automatically)
deadline: 30 days from the notice date to request a Collection Due Process hearing. After that, the levy can proceed.

name: CP297C
title: We levied your federal payments: your right to a hearing
what: The IRS has already levied federal payments due to your business, such as contractor payments, and is telling you of your right to a hearing. It is not a new bill.
common: Unpaid business taxes
A federal contractor with a tax balance
todo: Review the tax periods and amounts listed
If you disagree, submit Form 12153 to request a Collection Due Process hearing
Pay or set up a payment plan to stop future levies
deadline: Request a hearing by the date in the notice.

name: CP91
title: Final notice before levy on Social Security benefits
what: The IRS intends to take (levy) up to 15% of your Social Security benefits to pay your tax debt. This is a bill, and it gives you the right to a hearing before the levy starts.
common: Unpaid balance after earlier notices
No payment plan in place
todo: Request a Collection Due Process hearing with Form 12153 within 30 days
Set up a payment plan, an offer in compromise (a settlement for less), or ask for hardship status if you can't pay
Ask about penalty relief (reasonable cause, or first-time abatement if it wasn't applied automatically)
deadline: 30 days from the notice date to request a Collection Due Process hearing. After that, the levy on your benefits can begin.

name: CP92 / CP242
title: We took your state refund: your right to a hearing
what: The IRS took (levied) your state tax refund to pay federal tax you owe, and is telling you of your right to a hearing. CP92 goes to individuals and CP242 to businesses. It is not a new bill.
common: Unpaid federal tax balance
No payment plan in place
todo: Review the amount taken and the balance left
If you disagree, file Form 12153 within 30 days to request a hearing
Pay or set up a payment plan to stop further levies
deadline: 30 days from the notice date to request a hearing.

name: CP515
title: Reminder: we have no record of your tax return
what: The IRS has no record of a prior-year return you were required to file. It is not a bill, but it is an early step toward the IRS figuring your tax for you.
common: A return was never filed
A return was filed under the wrong Social Security number
todo: File the return right away
If you already filed or didn't need to, explain on Form 15103 by mail, fax or your IRS online account
Keep copies of everything you send
deadline: Respond by the date on the notice. If you don't, the IRS may prepare a return for you (CP2566).

name: CP516
title: Second reminder: we have no record of your tax return
what: A second reminder that the IRS has no record of one or more prior-year returns. It is not a bill.
common: A return was never filed
A return was lost or filed under the wrong number
todo: File the missing returns right away
If you already filed or didn't need to, explain on Form 15103
Get help if several years are missing
deadline: Respond by the date on the notice. If you don't, the IRS may prepare a return for you (CP2566).

name: CP518I
title: Final reminder: we have no record of your tax return
what: The final reminder that the IRS has no record of one or more prior-year returns. If you don't respond, the IRS will prepare a return for you based on information it has, usually with a higher tax. It is not a bill.
common: Earlier non-filing reminders weren't answered
A return was never filed
todo: File the missing returns immediately
If you already filed or didn't need to, explain on Form 15103
Get help if several years are missing
deadline: Respond by the date on the notice. Next comes a substitute return and proposed tax (CP2566).

name: CP518B
title: Final reminder: your business didn't file a return
what: The final reminder that the IRS has no record of a required business tax return. It is not a bill.
common: A return was never filed
A return filed under a different business name or EIN
todo: File the return right away, electronically if you can
Return the response form
If you filed more than 4 weeks ago, or under a different name or EIN, still return the response form
deadline: Respond by the date on the notice. If you don't, the IRS may prepare the return for you and assess tax and penalties.

name: CP2005
title: We accepted your information: no change
what: The IRS closed its review of income that didn't match its records and isn't making any changes. It is not a bill.
common: You answered a CP2000 or CP2501 with an explanation the IRS accepted
The income was already reported on your return
todo: You may not need to reply, but check the notice against your records and keep it on file
Keep the notice with your tax records
Contact the IRS if a later notice contradicts this one
deadline: No response required.

name: CP2006
title: We received your response and are reviewing it
what: The IRS received your reply about income that didn't match its records and is reviewing it. It is not a bill.
common: You answered a CP2000 or CP2501
You sent documents disputing proposed changes
todo: You may not need to reply now, but read the notice carefully and keep it with your records
Make a note to follow up if you don't hear back
Keep copies of what you sent
deadline: No response required.

name: CP2057
title: You may need to amend your return
what: The IRS received income information from employers, banks or others that may not be on your return. It is not a bill; the IRS is giving you the chance to correct it yourself.
common: A missed 1099 or W-2
Income reported on a form the IRS didn't match to your return
todo: Compare the income listed to your return
If the information is right and missing, file an amended return (Form 1040-X)
If it's wrong, ask the payer to correct it
deadline: Act by the date on the notice, if one is shown. Correcting it now can avoid a later proposed tax change.

name: CP2566
title: We figured your tax because you didn't file
what: You didn't file a return, so the IRS prepared one for you using income reported by employers, banks and others, and is proposing tax, penalties and interest. It is a proposal, not a bill yet, and it usually overstates what you owe.
common: Unanswered non-filing reminders
A return that was never filed
todo: File your actual return right away; it usually results in lower tax
If you agree with the IRS figures, sign and return the response form
If you had no filing requirement, call the number on the notice
Ask about penalty relief (reasonable cause, or first-time abatement if it wasn't applied automatically)
deadline: Respond by the date on the notice. If you don't, a Statutory Notice of Deficiency (CP3219N) follows.

name: Letter 226J
title: Proposed health coverage penalty for employers
what: The IRS is proposing an Affordable Care Act penalty (the employer shared responsibility payment) because it believes your business, as an employer with 50 or more full-time employees (including full-time equivalents), didn't offer qualifying health coverage. It is a proposal, not a bill.
common: A full-time employee got a premium tax credit on the Marketplace
Errors in the codes on Forms 1095-C
Coverage that didn't meet affordability or minimum value rules
todo: Review your Forms 1095-C and the employee list the IRS sent
Respond with Form 14764, and Form 14765 to correct any employee details
Explain any coverage offers or safe harbors that apply
If you disagree after the response, you can ask for an Appeals review
deadline: Respond by the date in the letter, at least 90 days for letters issued from 2025. If you don't, the IRS assesses the penalty (CP220J).

name: Letter 950
title: 30-day letter: proposed audit changes
what: After a field audit you didn't agree with, the IRS is proposing changes, usually more tax and possibly penalties. You have 30 days to take the case to the IRS Independent Office of Appeals. It is a proposal, not a bill.
common: Disagreement with the audit findings
Documents that didn't support deductions or income
todo: Read the audit report carefully
File a written protest within 30 days to go to Appeals
Ask whether any accuracy penalty can be removed for reasonable cause
If you agree, sign the agreement form
deadline: 30 days from the letter date to file a protest. Otherwise a Statutory Notice of Deficiency follows.

name: Letter 3172
title: A tax lien was filed: your right to a hearing
what: The IRS filed a Notice of Federal Tax Lien, a public claim against your property for unpaid tax, and is telling you of your right to a hearing. It relates to the balance you already owe.
common: Unpaid balance after earlier notices
No payment plan in place
todo: Request a Collection Due Process hearing with Form 12153 by the date in the letter
Ask about lien withdrawal, discharge or subordination (options that remove or limit the lien)
Pay in full or set up a payment plan
deadline: Request a hearing by the date in the letter, about 30 days. After that, the lien stays and levies can follow.

name: Letter 2205 / 2205-A
title: Your return was selected for an in-person audit
what: The IRS is starting an in-person (field) audit. Letter 2205-A lists the items being examined, and Letter 2205-D is used for partnerships. It is not a bill.
common: Selection for audit based on the return's figures
Large or unusual deductions or business losses
todo: Call to schedule the first meeting within 14 calendar days
If you want someone to represent you, sign Form 2848 (Power of Attorney)
Start gathering the records the auditor will ask for in a document request (Form 4564)
deadline: Call within 14 days to schedule. The audit goes ahead whether or not you respond.

name: Letter 692
title: Proposed audit changes: 15 days to respond
what: The IRS is proposing more changes to your return, usually more tax. You can agree or ask for an Appeals review. It is a proposal, not a bill.
common: Disagreement with audit findings
Additional issues found during the audit
todo: Review the proposed changes
Sign the form if you agree
If you disagree, file a protest within 15 days to go to Appeals
Ask about penalty relief (reasonable cause, or first-time abatement if it wasn't applied automatically)
deadline: 15 days from the letter date. Otherwise a Statutory Notice of Deficiency follows.

name: Letter 531
title: Statutory Notice of Deficiency
what: The IRS has determined you owe more tax and is formally telling you of your right to challenge it in U.S. Tax Court. It is a proposal, not a bill yet.
common: Audit changes you didn't agree to
No response to earlier audit letters
todo: Decide whether you agree with the changes
If you disagree, file a petition with the U.S. Tax Court before the deadline
Ask whether any penalties can be removed
deadline: 90 days from the notice date to petition Tax Court (150 days if addressed to you outside the U.S.). The deadline cannot be extended.

name: Letter 1153
title: Proposed personal penalty for unpaid payroll taxes
what: The IRS is proposing to hold you personally responsible for payroll taxes withheld from employees that your business didn't pay (the trust fund recovery penalty). It is a proposal, not a bill yet.
common: Payroll taxes withheld but not paid to the IRS
You had authority over which bills got paid
todo: Review whether you were actually responsible and knew the taxes weren't paid
File an appeal within 60 days if you disagree
Ask about mediation to settle the dispute faster
deadline: 60 days from the mailing date to appeal (75 days if addressed to you outside the U.S.). Otherwise the penalty is assessed against you personally.

name: CP3219N
title: Statutory Notice of Deficiency for an unfiled return
what: You didn't file a return, so the IRS figured your tax and is formally telling you of your right to challenge it in U.S. Tax Court. It is a proposal, not a bill yet, and it usually overstates the tax.
common: No response to a CP2566
A return that was never filed
todo: File your actual return right away; it often lowers the tax
If you disagree, petition the U.S. Tax Court before the deadline
If you agree, sign and return the form
Ask about penalty relief (reasonable cause, or first-time abatement if it wasn't applied automatically)
deadline: 90 days from the notice date to petition Tax Court (150 days if addressed to you outside the U.S.). The deadline cannot be extended.

name: CP220J
title: Employer health coverage penalty: bill
what: The IRS has assessed the Affordable Care Act employer penalty (the employer shared responsibility payment). This is a bill, and interest runs from the notice date.
common: No response to Letter 226J or Letter 227
Appeals or the IRS kept the penalty after review
todo: Check the amount against your Letter 226J and 227 records
Pay, or set up a payment plan
Follow the notice instructions if you want to challenge the penalty
deadline: Pay by the date on the notice. More balance-due notices follow if you don't.

name: Letter 227
title: Update on your employer health coverage penalty
what: The IRS is answering your Letter 226J response. Letter 227-J confirms the agreed penalty, 227-K closes it with no penalty, 227-L shows a reduced amount, 227-M keeps the penalty unchanged, and 227-N shows the Appeals result. It is not a bill.
common: You responded to Letter 226J
Appeals finished reviewing your case
todo: Check which version (227-L, 227-M, 227-N) you received
For 227-L or 227-M, agree on the response form, or disagree with an explanation and a revised Form 14765
For 227-M you can also request an Appeals meeting
For 227-N, no reply is needed
deadline: Respond by the date in the letter. If you don't, the IRS bills the penalty (CP220J).

name: LT39
title: Reminder: overdue balance or missing returns
what: A reminder that you have an overdue tax balance, missing returns, or both, and that the IRS may file a tax lien. This is a bill.
common: Unpaid balance after earlier notices
Returns not filed
A payment plan that ended
todo: Pay by the date on the notice, or pay what you can and set up a payment plan (online if you owe under $50,000)
File any missing returns listed
If you can't pay basic living expenses, ask about hardship status
Ask about penalty relief (reasonable cause, or first-time abatement if it wasn't applied automatically)
deadline: Pay by the date on the notice. Ignoring it risks a lien, a levy on wages or bank accounts, and certification that can affect your passport.
